title: Running Out: Meet IPv6
about: Why we ran short of addresses, and the longer kind that fixes it.

cards.prompt:
The free supply of [[IPv4]] addresses ran out in the 2010s, and [[NAT]] is only a workaround.

What would **really** fix the shortage?

options.text: A new kind of address with far more bits
Switching devices off at night to share addresses
options.nudge: Billions of devices stay on day and night: what limits how many addresses exist at all?

options.text: Shorter addresses, so each takes up less room
options.nudge: Fewer bits mean fewer patterns, so shorter addresses would give fewer, not more.

cards.explanation: Each extra bit doubles the patterns, so the fix is far longer addresses: **IPv6**, version 6 of the Internet [[Protocol]]. Shorter addresses give fewer, and switching off can't free enough.
cards.hint: IPv4 is 32 bits: what decides how many addresses a set of bits can make?

cards.title: 128 bits, written in hex
cards.body:
That fix is **IPv6**: **128-[[bit]]** addresses, four times as long as [[IPv4]]. Most devices have both.

It's written in [[hex]]: 8 groups of 4 digits, split by colons. `2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0001` shortens to `2001:db8::1`, where `::` stands for a run of zero groups.

cards.prompt: Each group in an [[IPv6]] address has 4 [[hex]] digits. How many **bits** is one group?
cards.hint: Each hex digit stands for 4 bits.
cards.explanation: Each hex digit is 4 bits, so a group is 4 × 4 = **16 bits**, and 8 groups make the whole 128.
cards.nudge: A group has 4 hex digits of 4 bits each: multiply.

cards.prompt: Written out in full, how many [[hex]] digits does an [[IPv6]] address have?
cards.hint: Count the groups and the digits in each, or start from the 128 bits.
cards.explanation: 8 groups × 4 digits = **32**, the same as 128 bits ÷ 4. In binary it would take all 128 digits, which is why IPv6 is written in hex.
cards.nudge: Count every group, not just one, or divide 128 bits by the bits in one hex digit.

cards.prompt: Match each value to what it is.
cards.explanation: IPv4 uses decimal numbers with **dots**, IPv6 hex groups with **colons**. `example.com` is a name, `11000000` is 8 bits, and `C8` has a hex letter.
cards.hint: Is each value split by dots or colons, and which digits or letters does it use?
cards.nudge: IPv4 is decimal with dots and IPv6 is hex with colons; the rest aren't addresses.

cards.prompt: A laptop lists two addresses: `192.168.1.42` and `2001:db8:1:2::42`. What's going on?

options.text: It has an IPv4 and an IPv6 address, and uses either
The second is just the first rewritten in hex
options.nudge: IPv6 is 128 bits and IPv4 only 32, so one can't be a copy: check the dots and colons.

options.text: One is the laptop's, and the other is the router's
options.nudge: Both are the laptop's own: which kind uses dots, and which uses colons?

cards.explanation: Dots mean [[IPv4]] and colons mean [[IPv6]]. Most devices have **both**, since much of the internet still only speaks IPv4; they're separate addresses, not one rewritten.
cards.hint: Are these two ways of writing one address, or two different addresses?

cards.prompt: [[IPv6]] has enough addresses for every device on Earth, many times over. Which [[IPv4]] workaround isn't needed now?

options.text: A whole home sharing one public address
Home routers linking homes to the internet
options.nudge: A home still needs a doorway to the internet: which trick existed only because addresses were scarce?

options.text: Names like example.com instead of numbers
options.nudge: People find names easier, and IPv6 is even harder to remember: what was IPv4 short of?

cards.explanation: Homes shared one address with [[NAT]] only because IPv4 ran short; with IPv6 every device can have its **own**. Routers still link networks, and names are still easier than hex.
cards.hint: Why was NAT invented in the first place?

cards.title: Recap
cards.body:
- **IPv6** fixes the shortage with **128-[[bit]]** addresses.
- They're 8 groups of [[hex]] digits, split by colons.
- Most devices use IPv4 and IPv6 side by side.
